extracted.intended_audience: jurors, judges, and practitioners in U.S. patent infringement trials (use of AIPLA model jury instructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for determining patent damages in U.S. litigation, covering when damages apply, types of recoverable damages, lost-profits analysis (Panduit), reasonable-royalty calculation (hypothetical negotiation and factors), apportionment, and related doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—Generally
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find that the accused [device/method] infringes any of the claims and those claims are not invalid, you must determine the amount of damages to be awarded. The Plaintiff must prove each element of its damages—including the amount—by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages must be adequate to compensate the Plaintiff for the infringement and put the Plaintiff in about the same financial position it would have been in absent the infringement. The damage award cannot be less than a reasonable royalty. You may not add anything to the amount of damages to punish an accused infringer or to set an example, nor add anything for interest. Instruction on damages does not imply court preference for outcome; consider damages only if you find valid, infringed claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date Damages Begin—Proof of Notice (marking or direct notice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The start date for damages is either a stipulated date or, if disputed, the date the Plaintiff first notified the Defendant of its claim for patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff can prove public notice by marking substantially all products that include the patented invention with the patent number (or marking with a free internet address linking product to patent). Licensees who use the invention must also mark substantially all their products. Alternatively, Plaintiff may directly notify Defendant with a specific charge; the notice-based damages period starts from the date Defendant received notice. If Plaintiff failed to provide effective public marking and did not properly provide direct notice before filing suit, damages are recoverable only from the lawsuit filing date. Plaintiff bears burden to prove notice by a preponderance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of Damages—Lost Profits
rubrics_metrics.description: One kind of damages is lost profits, the additional profits the patentee would have made if the defendant had not infringed (the 'but for' test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lost profits may include profits on lost direct sales and, under certain circumstances, profits lost from inability to sell related products or forced price reductions. Focus on profits allegedly lost by the Plaintiff, not profits made by the Defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of Damages—Established Royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: An established royalty is an amount the patentee has agreed to accept for licensing the patented invention through a consistent licensing practice outside of litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of prior license royalties can support an established-royalty recovery as an alternative to lost profits or reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of Damages—Reasonable Royalty (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the amount someone wanting to use the patented invention would have agreed to pay and the patent owner would have accepted; it is the minimum amount of damages a patent owner can receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable royalty damages must be based on the incremental value the patented invention adds to the end product. For products with both patented and unpatented features, determine the value added by the patented features and ensure the royalty base and rate reflect only that value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Profits—'But-For' Test
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove lost profits, the Plaintiff must show that, but for the Defendant’s infringement, the Plaintiff would have made additional profits by selling all or part of the sales that the Defendant made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove this by a preponderance. The jury must determine what purchasers would have done absent the infringement. Lost profits are profits allegedly lost by the Plaintiff, not defendant profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factors (framework for proving lost profits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff proves lost profits by showing each of the following by a preponderance: (1) demand for the patented product/method; (2) absence of acceptable non-infringing substitutes; (3) the Plaintiff had manufacturing and marketing ability to make the infringing sales; and (4) the amount of profit Plaintiff would have made but for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each Panduit factor must be proven by the more likely than not standard. The instructions explain and expand each factor below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor—Demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand for the patented product/method in the relevant market can be proven by significant sales of Plaintiff’s own patented product/method or significant sales of Defendant’s product/method covered by asserted claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To use Defendant's sales as proof, the products must be sufficiently similar to compete in the same market or market segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor—Absence of Acceptable Non-Infringing Substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether there were non-infringing, acceptable substitutes that competed with Defendant’s infringing product/method in the marketplace and the impact of such substitutes absent Defendant’s sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable substitute must have had one or more advantages of the patented invention important to actual buyers and must not infringe (i.e., not be licensed or not include all claimed features). The substitute must have been available during the damages period (it need not have actually sold). If not sold, Defendant must show by preponderance that competitors had necessary capability to make it. If customers would likely have purchased substitutes, Plaintiff is not entitled to lost profits for those sales. Even if only Plaintiff and Defendant had advantages, Plaintiff still must prove it would have made Defendant’s sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Profits—Market Share (when substitutes exist)
rubrics_metrics.description: If acceptable non-infringing substitutes existed, Plaintiff may be entitled to lost profits on a portion of Defendant’s sales equal to Plaintiff's market share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove by preponderance that it competed in the same market as Defendant and would have made the portion of infringing sales equal to its market share but for Defendant’s product. It is not necessary to prove only two suppliers existed, but must prove it would have sold that portion absent the infringer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor—Capacity (manufacturing/marketing ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must prove it had the manufacturing and marketing ability to supply the additional products or methods needed to make the sales it claims it lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof may include Plaintiff's own ability or someone working with Plaintiff who could supply the additional goods, and that Plaintiff more likely than not had the ability to market and sell them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor—Amount of Profit—Incremental Income Approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may calculate lost profits by computing lost sales and subtracting additional costs that would have been incurred to make those lost sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtract only costs that change with additional production (e.g., manufacturing, sales, packaging, shipping). Do not subtract fixed costs that do not change (taxes, insurance, rent, administrative overhead). Lost profits cannot be speculative, but need not be proven with unerring certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price Erosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may recover additional damages if, but for Defendant’s infringement, Plaintiff would have charged higher prices (or would not have lowered prices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proved by preponderance, award amount equal to difference between profits at higher price and profits at lower price actually earned. If awarding price-erosion damages, you may use the higher price to determine lost sales/lost profits but must account for any sales decrease due to higher price. Plaintiff need not have known Defendant's product infringed to recover price erosion damages if Plaintiff reduced price to compete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost Escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff can recover damages for increased costs (e.g., additional marketing) that occurred because of Defendant’s infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove by a preponderance that costs increased due to Defendant’s actions rather than other reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convoyed Sales (collateral products)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may claim lost profits for collateral products ordinarily sold with the patented product (convoyed sales).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To recover convoyed-sales damages Plaintiff must prove (1) it would have sold the collateral products but for the infringement, and (2) the collateral products and the patented product are so closely related that they act together for a common purpose. Damages for collateral products are calculated like lost profits on the primary product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Hypothetical Negotiation Method (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the royalty that would have resulted from a hypothetical license negotiation between Plaintiff and Defendant, assuming negotiation just before the infringement began, presuming the patent was valid and infringed and both parties were willing to license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume both parties had full knowledge of facts and circumstances surrounding the infringement at the time. The hypothetical negotiation is the standard means of measuring reasonable royalty damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Any royalties received by the licensor (established royalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any royalties received by the licensor for licensing of the patent-in-suit as evidence of an established royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports an established-royalty measure where there is consistent licensing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Comparable-license rates paid by Defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider rates paid by the Defendant to license other patents comparable to the patent-in-suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparable license rates can inform what Defendant would have paid in the hypothetical negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Nature and scope of the license
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the nature and scope of the license—exclusive vs. non-exclusive, territorial restrictions, or restrictions on whom the manufactured product may be sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License scope affects value and the royalty a licensee would accept or pay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Licensor’s policy/marketing to preserve exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the licensor’s established policy and marketing program to maintain its right to exclude by not licensing others or by granting licenses under conditions to preserve exclusivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A licensor’s practice of withholding licenses or limiting license rights can increase royalty value in the hypothetical negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Commercial relationship between licensor and licensee
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the commercial relationship between licensor and licensee (e.g., whether they are competitors in the same territory and line of business).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive relationships affect bargaining and royalty levels in the hypothetical negotiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Effect of patented product sales on other sales (collateral sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the effect of selling the patented product in promoting other sales of the licensee; the existing value of the invention to the licensor as a generator of sales of non-patented items, and the extent of such collateral sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value attributable to collateral sales can increase the reasonable royalty if the patented product drives additional non-patented sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Duration of patent and term of license
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the duration of the patent-in-suit and the term of the hypothetical license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer patent life or license term can increase royalty value; conversely, short remaining term can reduce royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Established profitability/commercial success/popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the established profitability of the product made under the patent, its commercial success, and its popularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial success and profitability are evidence of market value attributable to the invention and relevant to royalty calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Utility and advantages over prior modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the utility and advantages of the patented invention over the old modes or devices used to achieve similar results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovations that provide clear advantages can justify higher royalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Nature and commercial embodiment of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the nature of the patented invention, the character of its commercial embodiment as produced by or for the licensor, and the benefits to those who have used the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How the invention is embodied commercially and the benefits realized by users bear on its economic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Extent of Defendant’s use of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the extent to which the Defendant has made use of the invention and any evidence showing the value of that use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greater use by Defendant can support a higher royalty reflecting value extracted from the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Portion of profit or selling price customary for such use
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the portion of the profit or of the selling price that may be customary in the particular business or comparable businesses to allow for the use of the invention or analogous inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry customs for splitting profits or price components for licensed technology are relevant to a reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Apportionment—portion of profit arising from the patented invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the portion of the profit that arises from the patented invention itself as opposed to profit arising from unpatented features, manufacturing process, business risks, or improvements added by the accused infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate only the profit attributable to the patented features when calculating a royalty; do not attribute unrelated profits to the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Opinion testimony of qualified experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider opinion testimony of qualified experts regarding reasonable royalty and related economic valuations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert testimony is admissible evidence to inform the jury's determination of a reasonable royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Hypothetical agreement amount/prudent licensee test
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the amount that a licensor and a licensee would have agreed upon at the time the infringement began if both sides had been reasonably and voluntarily trying to reach an agreement—the amount a prudent licensee would pay and a willing patentee would accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a synthesis factor capturing the hypothetical negotiation outcome constrained by commercial reasonableness for both parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Factor: Any other economic factor a prudent business person would consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any other economic factor that a normally prudent business person would, under similar circumstances, take into consideration in negotiating the hypothetical license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This catch-all permits consideration of other relevant economic evidence not listed explicitly, if properly supported by the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution/Apportionment (royalty base and rate must reflect patented value)
rubrics_metrics.description: The damages must be based on the value attributable to the patented technology distinct from unpatented features or other factors (marketing, Defendant’s size, market position).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The royalty base must be closely tied to the invention; it is not appropriate to pick an overly large royalty base and offset by a low rate, nor pick too small a base and offset by a high rate. The combination of base and rate must reflect value attributable only to the patented invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire Market Value Rule (narrow exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally royalties should be based on the smallest salable unit that practices the patent and is closely related to the claimed invention; the entire market value rule is a narrow exception permitting damages based on the whole product only if the patented feature drives demand for the entire product or substantially creates the product's value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the smallest salable unit is multi-component with non-infringing features unrelated to the patented feature, damages must be limited to portion of value attributable to patented technology. To use entire-product revenue, Plaintiff must prove by preponderance that the patented feature 'substantially creates the value of the product' or drives customer demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Multiple Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: If Defendant infringed multiple patents, Plaintiff may be awarded separate royalties for each infringed patent and the jury may consider the number of patent licenses needed for the allegedly infringing product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider effect on the hypothetical negotiation of having to pay royalties for multiple licenses; separate royalty awards for each patent are permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Timing (what information to consider in hypothetical negotiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages are based on what the parties to the hypothetical license negotiations would have agreed upon just before the infringement began, not by hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence relevant to the negotiation is not necessarily limited to facts on or before the hypothetical negotiation date; you may consider information the parties would have foreseen or estimated at the time, which may include usage after infringement started, license agreements entered shortly after the negotiation date, profits earned by the infringer, and non-infringing alternatives, where properly supported by the evidence.
